title: Hyderabad Leads India's Record GCC Boom With 40 New Centres
excerpt: India added 111 new global capability centres in the first eight months of 2026, already beating 2025's full-year record — and Hyderabad took the top slot ahead of Bengaluru.
body:
• India added 111 greenfield global capability centres in the first eight months of 2026, already beating 2025's full-year record of 100 — putting the country on pace for an all-time high year.
  • Hyderabad led the 2026 intake with 40 new centres, ahead of Bengaluru's 30 — the first year the southern rival has taken the top slot on new GCC additions.
  • The new centres are expected to create 70,000–75,000 jobs and generate $2.5–2.8 billion in annualised revenue and foreign exchange.
  • A separate FICCI-Anarock report pegs Hyderabad's total GCC base at roughly 515 centres employing over 3 lakh people, with 50–70 more expected within a year.

India's global capability centre boom is running at a record pace. The country added 111 greenfield GCCs in the first eight months of 2026, already surpassing the 100 new centres added in all of 2025, per a report by UnearthIQ cited by The Hindu BusinessLine. At the current run rate, Moneycontrol projects 125–130 new centres by year-end — which would make 2026 the strongest year on record.

Of this year's new centres, 40 landed in Hyderabad, 30 in Bengaluru, 18 in Pune, 8 in Chennai, 7 in Mumbai and 4 in Delhi-NCR — the first year Hyderabad has taken the top slot on new GCC additions.

Hyderabad's playbook

The FICCI-Anarock report "Hyderabad: The Rise of a Global Capability Powerhouse," released September 10, puts Hyderabad's total GCC base at roughly 515 centres as of March 2026, employing more than 3 lakh people — over 70 added in FY25, the highest among compared cities — and projects 50–70 more within a year, creating 75,000-plus high-skilled jobs over three to five years.

The wins are tangible. Vanguard opened a Global Value Centre at HITEC City; Costco is ramping toward roughly 1,000 hires; L'Oréal is setting up what it calls the world's first beauty-tech GCC; and six BFSI greenfield wins arrived in the first half of 2026, including UBS (3,000 hires), CIBC (2,000-plus), Hartford (~1,200), LPL Financial (700), Nationwide (~500) and Zurich Insurance.

"The sustained leasing momentum reflects the deepening of Hyderabad's GCC ecosystem and the increasing preference of global enterprises to establish larger and more sophisticated operations in the city."

— Anuj Puri, Chairman, Anarock Group

GCC office leasing in Hyderabad hit 4.5 million sq ft in 2025 versus 1.9 million in 2021, and crossed 3 million sq ft in the first half of 2026 alone. Hi-tech companies led the 2026 intake with 28 new centres, followed by manufacturing (20), professional services (12), BFSI (10) and healthcare/pharma (10).

The reverse-migration pull

The GCC boom is unfolding alongside a measurable shift in diaspora talent flows. A Blind survey of 1,276 verified professionals found 53% had witnessed reverse migration to India, with US companies increasingly absorbing returning engineers into their India GCCs — sometimes, one quoted Google professional said, at a fifth of equivalent US pay. The 2026 H-1B visa changes and the $100,000 fee have added a policy push, and an Emeritus survey found 48% of prospective study-abroad students say their interest in studying overseas has declined, with the US taking the sharpest hit.

The pull is strongest in scarce skills. Quess Corp reports a 42% skill gap in AI and data roles within BFSI GCCs is driving 1.5x–2.5x salary premiums, and GCC pay runs about 30% above average. But the picture is not uniformly rosy: the same Blind survey found 51% of respondents said hiring opportunities in India had actually declined over the past year — the return wave benefits employers more than returnees on pay, and the job pipeline lags the growth of centres.

"India's own growth and evolving opportunities are making the decision increasingly attractive. Rather than handling basic back-office work, local firms and GCCs are now driving core AI research, cloud infrastructure, and flagship products."

— Lakshmi Iyer, Chief Client Officer and Chairperson, StudyIn India

Scale and what's next

Nationally, Nasscom-Zinnov data puts India's GCC base at over 2,100 centres employing about 2.36 million professionals, with sector revenue near $98 billion in FY26 and projected to reach about $108 billion in FY27. Bengaluru still leads on absolute stock with roughly 29% of the base, while Hyderabad has risen from 12% in FY24 to 14% — FICCI-Anarock, using a different methodology, credits it with about 20%. Either way, the trajectory is clear: India's GCC sector is no longer a back-office story but a frontier for AI research, product engineering and global financial operations.

For the diaspora, the signal is practical. GCCs offer one of the cleanest landing paths back into India's job market — globally branded employers, dollar-grade work, and in the hottest skills, pay that narrows the gap with US levels. The watch item: whether the job pipeline keeps pace with the growth of centres, or whether, as the surveys warn, the boom outruns hiring.
nri_angle: India's GCC boom offers returning-NRI tech professionals globally branded employers and dollar-grade work, with salary premiums narrowing the gap to US levels in scarce skills.
author: Diaspora Desk
